newsitem.title: UK: EMU jitters shift spotlight from Britain's Blair.
newsitem.headline: EMU jitters shift spotlight from Britain's Blair.

text.p: When Tony Blair stormed to power in his landslide British election victory on May 1, the rest of Europe breathed a sigh of relief.
No longer would the European Union be held up by a Eurosceptic Conservative administration bent on confrontation.
The only question was whether Blair could be ready in time for the Amsterdam summit, called to redraw the group's treaties.

Six weeks later and all the signs are that Blair will not only be ready, but will get his own way on the main issues that determine whether his appearance at the summit is judged a success or a failure at home.

Foreign Secretary Robin Cook told parliament this week: "We can return from Amsterdam not just having done a good deal for Britain but having obtained a better deal for Britain than the previous government could ever hope to have achieved."
The only problem is, the spotlight has moved on.

The new French Socialist government's demand for more time to examine the stability pact designed to underpin European economic and monetary union (EMU) has made the EU's planned single currency the hot issue and focused attention on the Franco-German alliance.
Blair, trying to capitalise on the warm glow that surrounded his first summit meeting with his fellow EU leaders at Noordwijk a month ago, is pressing on with his agenda.

He met French President Jacques Chirac on Wednesday night and aides said he was busily calling fellow leaders -- German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, followed by Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen and France's Socialist premier Lionel Jospin on Thursday -- to set out his demands for Amsterdam.

Blair's top demand -- a guarantee that Europe would not have any say over Britain's borders -- was designed to show voters at home that the new Labour government would be just as tough at defending the country's interests in Europe.
In return, Blair has said he is prepared to accept more majority voting and to sign up to the social chapter setting out moves to standardise worker protection across the bloc.

All the signs are -- despite the attempts of some senior British officials to build up the border question into a battle which will prove Blair's negotiating mettle -- that the borders issue will be resolved to London's satisfaction.
But the issue is in any case increasingly a sideshow to the pregnancy pains of the single currency.
Blair is eyeing this cautiously.
Already having made clear Britain is highly unlikely to be in the first wave of the currency if it goes ahead on time in 1999, the Labour government is on the sidelines.
But senior aides are keen to dismiss any suggestion that Blair -- for whom the single currency pressure is off -- may be "revelling" in the problems of others.
He wants to be involved, they say. "Sitting on the sidelines causing grief for others while having ruled out participation ourselves would be pointless," said one senior aide on Thursday.
And Cook said in an interview for Friday's issue of the left-leaning New Statesman: "For Britain to attempt to veto a single currency would make it the fall guy of Europe for everyone else to blame."
But others warn that Blair needs to get involved.
"He is watching -- not gloating, but not helping, either," said Andrew Marr, the pro-Blair editor of the Independent newspaper, of the single currency debate.
"He is standing by as Europe's pet project goes into purple-faced seizure."

Blair's message, laid out at Noordwijk, that Europe has lost touch with its citizens and needs to do concrete things like boosting employment to enthuse its citizens, is not new. But it is striking a chord with other European leaders.
The problem is, Blair has to be seen to be at the heart of Europe to win backing for his drive to use Europe to boost jobs and to make the bloc seem relevant to its citizens.
So far, commentators say, Blair's words have not been matched by his actions. Amsterdam could be a key test -- even if most eyes will be elsewhere.
